content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler crunchies are soft, crunchy snacks specially designed for children aged 12 months to 3 years. They are made from whole grains, fruits and vegetables, without artificial colours, flavours or preservatives. The snack is easy to chew and helps develop independent eating skills.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The snacks are shaped into small “finger‑size” pieces that are easy for little hands to hold.
The formula includes whole grains such as oats and rice, plus dried fruit and vegetable purees.
One serving provides about 30 % of the daily vitamin C requirement for 1‑ to 3‑year‑olds.
Each batch is tested to ensure no small particles that could increase choking risk.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and can be opened with one hand.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system development in toddlers.

items.title: Contains dietary fibre
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps establish a beneficial gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Minimal added sugar helps foster healthy taste preferences early on.

items.title: Supports bone growth
items.content: The snack provides calcium and vitamin D, which contribute to strong bone development.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Children with known allergies to wheat, oats or rice should avoid this product.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Despite the shape, small pieces may still pose a choking risk for children under 12 months.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The product contains a modest amount of salt; consider this if the child's diet is low‑sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Offer 2–3 pieces as a snack between meals. The crunchies can be served with milk, yogurt or fruit puree. Keep them dry so they stay crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the original package in a cool, dry place. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container. Shelf life is 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken wings are tender pieces of poultry slowly cooked in a flavorful sauce with vegetables and spices. They have a juicy texture, rich taste, and a mild hint of heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewed wings are common in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines.
Stewing retains more nutrients compared with deep‑frying.
Chicken wings are a popular snack at sporting events and buffets.
Traditional stewing sauces may include tomato paste, soy sauce, honey, and spices.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wings supply niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: They contain iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Stewed wings fit well into low‑carb dietary plans.

items.title: Provides collagen
items.content: Slow cooking releases collagen from bones and skin, beneficial for skin and joints.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is salty, monitor intake, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Chicken must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed wings can be served as a main dish, added to salads, sandwiches, or enjoyed as a snack. Reheat quickly in a microwave or skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag at –18 °C, where they remain good for 2‑3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat oatmeal cookie is a light, crunchy snack made from whole oat flakes, whole‑grain flour, a modest amount of vegetable oil and sweeteners. The recipe omits raisins, making it suitable for those who avoid dried fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat flakes retain most of the fiber and beta‑glucans beneficial for heart health.
The cookies are baked at a lower temperature, preserving a crisp texture without excess oil.
Fat reduction is achieved by replacing part of the oil with apple puree, keeping moisture.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.
Oatmeal cookies are often used in weight‑loss meal plans.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oat flakes provide soluble fiber that helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Reduced oil makes the cookie less caloric than traditional versions.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans support cholesterol reduction and immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats supply thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber promotes intestinal motility and regular bowel movements.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although refined sugar is reduced, a small amount of sweetener remains.

items.title: Risk of over‑consumption
items.content: The crunchy texture may lead to rapid eating of large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt or muesli, or use it as a base for dessert tartlets. Keep it dry to maintain crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container at room temperature, away from direct sunlight. For extended shelf life, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption.

egg-sandwich-on-bagel-with-sausage.title: Egg Sandwich on Bagel with Sausage

content.title: About
content.content: The egg sandwich on a bagel with sausage is a satisfying breakfast or snack. A freshly boiled egg, flavorful sausage, and a lightly toasted bagel create a balanced mix of protein, fat, and carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and are traditionally boiled before baking.
Eggs are one of the most affordable complete protein sources, containing all essential amino acids.
The sausage can vary—from classic ham to smoked Polish kielbasa—allowing flavor customization.
The combination of a creamy yolk and soft bread makes the sandwich especially filling.
This sandwich is commonly served in fast‑food cafés and school cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and sausage provide a high amount of complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while sausage adds niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Sausage, especially beef varieties, offers heme iron that helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The bagel supplies quick‑release carbs that give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The blend of protein, fat, and carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some sausage types are high in saturated fat, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs should avoid this sandwich to prevent reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, preferably cut in half. It pairs well with sliced vegetables, leafy greens, or a favorite sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep the bagel in an airtight container to prevent it from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood paella is a classic Spanish dish made with Bomba rice, olive oil, saffron, vegetables and a mix of seafood such as shrimp, mussels, squid and fish. The dish is known for its aromatic broth and the crispy bottom layer called “socarrat.”

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Paella originates from Valencia, where it is traditionally cooked over an open fire in a wide, shallow pan called a “paellera.”
Saffron, which gives the dish its golden hue, is one of the most expensive spices in the world.
The original Valencian paella uses local ingredients: chicken, rabbit, garbanzo beans and green beans “ferra.”
The seafood version is called “paella de marisco” and is popular in coastal regions of Spain.
Paella is often a communal dish, prepared for celebrations and family gatherings.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid, fish) provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fish and shellfish contain EPA and DHA, which support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bomba rice is a slow‑digesting carbohydrate that offers steady blood‑sugar levels and lasting satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thanks to the seafood and saffron, the dish supplies B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Paella provides iron, zinc, selenium and iodine, nutrients that aid the immune system and thyroid function.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or fish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Broths and seasonings can be salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Certain seafood can accumulate cadmium or mercury; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich due to oil and rice, so portions should be moderated for weight control.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve paella hot, straight from the pan. Eat with a fork or spoon, mixing rice with the seafood. It is often garnished with lemon wedges, fresh parsley and a pinch of smoked paprika.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of broth or water to restore moisture. Freeze only for up to 1 month after cooling the dish completely.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork bacon is salted, smoked or cured pork belly that has been cured, optionally smoked, and sometimes pre‑cooked. It can be sold fresh, smoked, or dry‑cured, and is often ready for quick frying or grilling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon is a staple in many cuisines, from American breakfasts to European charcuterie boards.
Smoked bacon gets its distinctive flavor from wood smoke generated during a slow‑smoking process.
Cured bacon is typically aged for several weeks, which deepens flavor and extends shelf life.
Pork bacon is rich in protein and saturated fat, making it an energy‑dense food.
In some cultures bacon is served in ultra‑thin slices, crisped to a crunchy texture.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Bacon provides a substantial amount of complete protein needed for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Bacon supplies iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in bacon helps immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Natural creatine can aid muscle strength and endurance.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Bacon is salty, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Nitrites/Nitrates
items.content: Processing often uses nitrites that can form potentially harmful compounds when over‑cooked.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to pork proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bacon is very calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon is typically sliced thin and fried until crisp. It can be added to salads, sandwiches, soups, pasta, and potato dishes. Dry‑cured bacon can be eaten as a snack, while smoked bacon works as a flavorful garnish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bacon refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Fresh and smoked bacon should be used within 5–7 days; cured bacon lasts up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor, discoloration, or slimy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) are edible fruits of the tomato plant, widely used in cooking. When added to an omelet they give the dish a bright colour, juiciness and a mild tang, while boosting its nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes are botanically berries, although they are treated as vegetables in the kitchen.
Ripe tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Tomatoes were first domesticated in South America over 2,000 years ago.
There are more than 10,000 tomato varieties, differing in shape, size and flavour.
Tomatoes can be enjoyed raw or cooked; heat brings out a sweeter taste.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a carotenoid linked to reduced risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories, making them a good addition to weight‑control meals.

items.title: Provides dietary fibre
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or their juice.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of tomatoes can aggravate heartburn in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic tomatoes, rinse them thoroughly to reduce any pesticide residue.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dice or slice tomatoes and add them to the omelet a few minutes before it finishes cooking, allowing them to warm through while retaining shape. For a sweeter flavour, you can briefly sauté the tomatoes first.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh tomatoes at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, for up to 5–7 days. Ripe tomatoes that will be used later can be kept in the refrigerator, though this may affect their texture.
